PERM permanent labor certification · FY2013-FY2024

Who the public sector sponsors

A university hiring a physicist from abroad surprises nobody. A state corrections department sponsoring a psychiatrist for permanent residence is the same legal instrument used for a different purpose, and almost nobody has looked at it.

This page reads the Department of Labor's PERM disclosure files for FY2013-FY2024 and keeps every certified filing by an employer that is a university, a school district or an agency of a state government. It shows the distributions rather than a league table, because the shape of a sector says more than its top ten.

A PERM filing is a request. The employer asks the Department of Labor for permission to sponsor permanent residence, after testing the local labor market as the regulation requires. A certified filing means the request was granted. It does not mean a person was hired, and nothing on this page says any employer or worker broke a rule.

The three sectors

Each sector is classified from the employer's own name, by rule, not by hand. A name that reads as a school is tested as a school before it is tested as a university, so a university-run high school lands in the K–12 sector and not the other way round.

State agencies

Departments of a state government. The smallest sector by far, and the one a reader is most likely to find unexpected, because these are posts inside the machinery of a state.

The other half of this

This page counts permanent-residence filings. The H-1B page counts the temporary work visas, which are far more numerous and run from FY2009. It can tell you how many and which agencies. It cannot tell you who: the H-1B files do not link a nationality to an employer. That is the one thing this page can do, and it is why the two belong side by side.

Employer names come through as the filer typed them, and the federal files truncate long ones. Two spellings of the same department appear as two rows where the truncation differs. Citizenship is listed in full for each role, not topped, because one filing from an unexpected country is the thing worth finding.

Utilities: power, gas and water

Electric generation and distribution, natural gas, water and sewage. This sector is found by industry code rather than by name, because 'Electric' in a company name usually means it makes equipment rather than power. Most of it is investor-owned, not public, and the page marks which is which rather than quietly dropping the private ones: they run the same grid.

Most of the mismatch is one country

Of the 2,241 filings where citizenship and birth country differ, the largest single citizenship is Canada, with 896 of them. These are people who emigrated once already, took a second nationality, and then moved again. The pattern is a staging post, not a discrepancy.

Method and limits

Built from 12 PERM disclosure files published by the Office of Foreign Labor Certification. Every figure on this page is computed at build time from those files.

  • A PERM certification is an employer asking to sponsor someone for permanent residence after testing the local labor market. It is not a hire, not an admission, and not an H-1B petition.
  • Many of these workers were already in the job on another visa. The visa_held field says which one.
  • Citizenship is published for FY2013 onward and was removed from FY2025, when the form lost every worker field at once. Birth country runs FY2015 to FY2024. The series has ended.
  • No worker is named in the federal file and none is named here. Employer, job title, worksite and citizenship are all published disclosure.
  • Employers are matched on the name as filed, so one body can appear under several spellings and any single total is a floor.
  • Sponsoring a worker is lawful. Nothing here says otherwise.
  • The window ends at FY2024 because the Department of Labor stopped publishing the worker fields. The FY2025 and FY2026 files carry no citizenship, no country of birth and no class of admission. That is why this page cannot be brought up to date, and it is a change in what the government discloses, not a change in what employers filed.
  • Filings are counted once each, de-duplicated by case number, because the quarterly releases overlap and a case appears in more than one file.
  • A certified filing is permission to sponsor. It is not a hire, not a visa, and not a green card. Counting filings as people would overstate every figure here.
  • Sector membership is decided by the employer's name. A name that does not say what the employer is will not be found, so all three counts are floors.

Source: US DOL OFLC, PERM permanent labor certification disclosure files.
